name: PT Bukit Asam (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bukit Asam: Indonesia's state coal reserve, priced as if the cycle never turns
frontmatter.summary: We initiate on Bukit Asam, the state-owned miner controlled by the MIND ID holding, at BUY. The market is paying for the coal deck's own Newcastle path while ignoring a reserve base that lasts a generation, the rupiah cash-cost base, a restated earnings stream and a balance sheet carrying net cash and listed associate stakes. A weak rupiah and the deck's near-term price years lift the near-term cash flows; a Newcastle rollover and a thin per-tonne margin are the risks.
thesis: Bukit Asam's reserve base and its two port-and-rail systems give it a reserve life measured in decades, and the life-of-asset NAV values that at the coal deck's long-run marker, not at spot.
The realised price is calibrated on the last actual year and held flat, so no war-premium spike is carried into the long-run value; the upside is a cycle-position and balance-sheet story.
The state holding structure, the rupiah cost base and the dividend policy give a floor that is not in a spot-earnings multiple.

The market's implied through-cycle Newcastle price is a touch below the deck's own long-run marker, so the discount is to the near-term deck cash flows, the reserve life and the balance sheet rather than to a long-run price disagreement.
Risks are the thin per-tonne margin at trough prices, a domestic-demand and DMO policy squeeze, and the governance weight of a state-controlled, related-party-heavy revenue book.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Bukit Asam (Persero) Tbk with a **BUY** rating and a twelve-month target of **Rp5,358**, an expected return of **75.0%** against the last close of Rp3,280. Our through-cycle, life-of-asset DCF values the equity at Rp5,289 per share; the EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp3,906 and the dividend-capacity anchor Rp3,381, and the blend lands on the target [S5, S6, S7].

PTBA is Indonesia's only state-owned coal producer and one of its largest, held 65.9% by the MIND ID mining holding [S7]. It sold 45.43 Mt of coal in the last financial year from five managed mining areas feeding its own rail corridor and two large dedicated coal ports [S7]. The coal is medium-calorific and mostly sold domestically, so its realised price is a fraction of the seaborne Newcastle benchmark, and its cash costs are incurred and settled in rupiah while its revenue is dollar-denominated [S5, S7].

Our variant view is what the price does *not* carry. Working back from today's close, the reverse DCF solves a whole-path Newcastle multiplier just below parity (0.98), so the marker it implies at the deck's own long-run year sits a touch below the deck's long-run price of US$105.0 a tonne — the market already pays roughly the house long-run price path and appears to give little or nothing for a reserve base that lasts roughly a generation at the company's own sales rate, for the net cash and listed-associate stakes sitting on the June-2026 balance sheet, or for the restated, fuller depreciation charge that rebuilds the cash flow base [S5, S6, S7]. When we re-price the last actual year at its own benchmark, volume and realised ratio the model reproduces the LK's EBITDA to within a fraction of a percent; the residual in our calibration gate is the first forecast year's measured realised ratio and the rupiah translation step, explained below [S5].

What moves the value is the benchmark, the rupiah, and the volume-intensity of the cost base. The sensitivity grid in the valuation section shows that a tenth either way on the benchmark is worth far more than a tenth on volume; the exchange rate cuts both ways through the dollar revenue and the rupiah cost line.

Bukit Asam is one of the oldest coal enterprises in the archipelago, its Tanjung Enim pits worked since
the colonial era and nationalised after independence; it listed on the Jakarta exchange in the early
two-thousands. Indonesian thermal coal is a seaborne swing-supply industry: the country is among the
world's largest exporters, its product is mostly medium-calorific and sold into South Asia, East Asia
and South-East Asia, and its domestic power fleet consumes a mandated share of national output.

PTBA is an integrated Indonesian coal company. Its operating core is open-pit thermal-coal mining in South Sumatra around Tanjung Enim, with smaller operations in East Kalimantan, Riau and West Sumatra; the annual report counts five managed mining areas and three ports and puts the total mining-permit area at a fixed footprint across the group [S7]. The company holds its producing permits as Izin Usaha Pertambangan (IUP) Operasi Produksi, the Tanjung Enim Air Laya block under permit No. 94/1/IUP/PMDN/2020 [S7]. Its product slate runs from a low-calorific product up to a high-calorific one, with the bulk of the blend in the medium-calorific GAR range [S7].

The revenue mix is coal, with a smaller non-coal line that the last actual year put at a single-digit share of the total [S5]. Domestic sales took a little over half the last financial year's volume and exports the rest, with the largest export destinations in South Asia, Indochina and North-East Asia [S7]. Coal mining is the dominant profit pool; the group also operates coal transport and port infrastructure, a downstream and power arm including mine-mouth and mine-adjacent generation, and a green-business arm spanning plantation and agribusiness activities [S7]. The company is structured as a holding of operating subsidiaries; its largest mining-services subsidiary is majority-owned and the group's related-party revenue book is large because state entities are related parties under the Indonesian accounting standards [S5].

Volume grew in the last financial year: production and purchases reached 47.19 Mt, the highest in the company's history, and sales 45.43 Mt, both above the prior year's 43.28 Mt and 42.89 Mt respectively, though still short of the internal budget target [S7]. Sales are routed through long-term and spot contracts, and the company has run end-user agreements with the state power fleet priced off calorific value [S5]. Its strategy, stated in the annual report, is to monetise the reserve base through volume growth, to deepen downstream and power, and to keep extending its permits on time [S7]. The controlling shareholder is the state mining holding, and strategy is set with the holding's direction as well as the board's own review [S7].

A share buyback has been under review since late October 2026: management said it is studying the option among other corporate actions, that any decision would consider liquidity and working-capital needs, and that it would disclose to the regulator and the exchange if it proceeded [S2]. We treat it as a catalyst, not as value.

Indonesia's thermal-coal industry is a large, export-led swing supplier with a policy-managed domestic market. National production fell to 790 Mt in the last financial year from a higher level the year before, and PTBA's own output was a mid-single-digit share of it [S7]. The government manages supply through the annual work-and-budget plan (RKAB): through 2026 most of the national quota was approved at an aggregate level near the prior-year run-rate [S10], after an earlier proposal to tighten the ceiling sharply [S9]. PTBA's own RKAB was approved without a volume cut, and the company targets production and sales near the level it confirmed in October 2026 [S3, S4].

The domestic-market obligation requires producers to sell a quarter of output to the domestic market, with a standing price ceiling for power-station coal that sits above the company's realised price at present and therefore binds nothing in our base case [S5]. The royalty regime is the other structural lever: PTBA as an IUP holder pays the progressive production royalty set by government regulation, whose rate is banded on the government's coal reference price and which is higher on higher-calorific tonnage [S5].

Competitive position. PTBA is a mid-tier national producer by volume but a top-tier holder of reserves, with a reserve base the annual report puts in the billions of tonnes across its permits [S7]. Its advantage is integration: mine-mouth rail and river transport and two large dedicated coal ports, one of them among the largest in South-East Asia, which the company has been extending with a new coal-transport line [S7]. That logistics control is the moat — it lets PTBA move volume to the coast at a lower delivered cost than a mine without its own corridor — but the same integration makes it capital-heavy and exposes it to rail and port availability. Its weakness is product quality: the medium-calorific blend does not command the seaborne premium of high-calorific Australian coal, so its realised price is structurally discounted.

Five forces. Supplier power is moderate — the group self-performs some haulage and uses contracted mining services, and fuel and heavy equipment are imported; the intensity of the cost base is set by a strip ratio that the company reported slightly below its budget in the last actual year [S7]. Buyer power is high: the domestic power fleet is a mandated, price-capped customer and export buyers clear at index-linked prices. Substitutes are rising — gas and renewables in the domestic grid — but coal-fired capacity is still being added in South and South-East Asia. New entrants are effectively barred by the permit regime. Rivalry is moderate domestically and intense in the seaborne market, where Indonesian supply competes with Australian, Russian and Colombian tonnes.

The commodity frame. The house coal deck prices Newcastle f.o.b. through a mean-reverting path, with a near-term war-premium year folding back toward a long-run marker well below spot, and the government reference price following it down [S5 deck]. The macro desk's IDR view is mildly weakening, which translates dollar coal revenue into more rupiah against a rupiah cost base. Both are the frame this name is valued in, not inputs we re-forecast.

The seaborne thermal-coal price is among the most volatile in the commodity complex: it multiplies in
supply shocks and halves when Chinese and Indian output returns. Indonesian producers are price-takers
on the export market and regulated customers at home, so the industry's earnings are a leveraged bet on
the benchmark and on policy rather than on company-specific execution.

History. The last five fiscal years were a full cycle: a boom year, a second strong year, then two years of falling prices and, in the last actual year, a compression to a thin gross margin even as volumes rose [S5]. Total revenue in the last actual year was IDR42,651.7bn, against IDR42,765.0bn a year earlier — broadly flat, on higher volumes and a lower realised price, with coal the overwhelming share of it and a small non-coal line on top [S5]. The company's own report describes the last year as one in which the average selling price fell on weaker global benchmarks, with the volume gain offsetting it at the top line [S7].

Earnings quality and the depreciation restatement. This is the single most important correction to the street's data on PTBA. The consolidated statements are presented on the direct cash-flow method and carry no depreciation line in the cash-flow statement, so third-party data packs pick up only a fragment of the real charge. The audited accounts' own segment disclosure puts consolidated depreciation and amortisation at 2,014 IDR bn in the last actual year and 1,797 IDR bn in the year before [S5]. On the data pack's fragment the last actual year's EBITDA looks like a high-single-digit margin business; on the real charge it is a low-teens share of revenue, and the model restates history to the audited figure and rebuilds EBITDA from it [S5]. Everything we say about margins, cash conversion and the EV/EBITDA cross-check follows from that restatement. Our restated history is keyed to the audited consolidated statement line by line [S5]: revenue, cost of revenue and gross profit are the LK's own lines, and the operating-expense line is the LK's total operating expenses — 3,153 IDR bn in the last actual year and 2,867 IDR bn the year before — in place of the data pack's derived plug. The LK carries its net other income of 104 IDR bn as a separate line between operating expenses and operating profit, so the audited gross profit less that operating-expense line plus that net other income is the operating profit the model carries as EBIT and the restated history ties to the filing [S5].

Cost structure and the margin. Cash cost per tonne is the identity that drives the model: cost of revenues less the government royalty less the depreciation and amortisation charged inside it, divided by volume [S5]. That leaves a modelled rupiah cash operating cost per tonne which, set against a realised price struck from the FY2025A benchmark of US$108.4 a tonne and the calibrated realisation of 0.46, gives the thin per-tonne margin the last actual year showed. The cash cost is dominated by the non-mining items — the haulage, rail and port charges on a large transported volume — rather than by the strip-ratio input [S7]. Royalties to government were 4,323 IDR bn in the last actual year, about a tenth of revenue, the blended outcome of the calorie-banded IUP schedule across domestic, lower-calorific and export tonnes [S5].

Cash flow, capital spending and the balance sheet. Operating cash flow was strong relative to reported profit in the last actual year, and capital expenditure was 3,505 IDR bn, an investment peak roughly triple the prior year's 1,232 IDR bn, funding the new transport line and the downstream build [S5, S7]. Working capital is a modest negative at the group level, a small source of cash as the business scales [S5]. The group held a net cash position at the June-2026 interim date, with total debt of a small fraction of equity, and it carries significant equity-accounted investments in associates and joint ventures on the balance sheet [S6]. Capital allocation is dividend-led with a stated policy floor and a heavy reinvestment programme running alongside it [S7].

Forecasts. We take the company's own sales plan for the first forecast year and hold it flat thereafter, at the RKAB-approved level [S3, S4]. The realised price is the last actual year's ratio of asp to benchmark, held flat, so the deck's near-term price years flow through but no spike is baked into the long run. Costs are held at the last actual in real terms, then escalated with the currencies they are paid in: rupiah costs with Indonesian inflation, dollar benchmarks with US inflation, which is the nominal-consistent treatment the house method requires. The first forecast year reflects the deck's war-premium benchmark, so it is the top of the forecast range in prices, but it is *not* the top of the forecast range in realised price: the first-half actuals post-date the balance sheet and show a weaker ratio than the last actual year, so the first forecast year carries the measured ratio and the model returns to the last-actual calibration from the second forecast year [S2, S5, S6].

The first forecast year reconciled to the first-half actuals. The interim accounts put first-half coal revenue at 21,672 IDR bn on 21.10 Mt of sales — an average realised price well below the level first-year benchmark prices alone would imply — and first-half net profit at IDR2,650.0bn against the prior year's much weaker print [S6, S2]. We therefore do not take the first forecast year's realised price off the benchmark spike: we set the first forecast year's realised-to-benchmark ratio at the measured first-half ratio and revert to the last-actual year's calibration thereafter, on the view that a medium-calorific, domestic-heavy book does not carry a seaborne high-calorific war premium into its realised price. That step is what makes the second half of the first forecast year the heaviest half in the model — the deck's own price path rises sharply from the first half into the second, and the company's full-year volume target requires a second-half delivery well above the first half's — so the first forecast year's cash flow is back-loaded and the model shows a first-to-second-year step up in earnings rather than a smooth ramp [S3, S4, S6]. If the second-half delivery or the realised ratio disappoints the print, the first forecast year's earnings — and the dividend that sits on them — come in below the model, which is the single sensitivity we watch most closely [S2, S6].

The forecast therefore shows revenue, earnings and cash flow rising into the deck's near-term price year and then reverting with the benchmark, with the reserve life and the flat cost base holding the terminal years positive [S5 deck]. We do not model a terminal growth rate: the DCF runs on reserves and stops when marginal value turns negative, consistent with the coal peer set.

Why this method set. PTBA is a life-of-asset commodity producer, so the primary method is a life-of-reserve DCF at the coal deck's through-cycle prices, not a spot multiple. A cyclical valued on current-year earnings is the classic procyclical error; here the NAV is struck on the deck's mean-reverting Newcastle path, and the EV/EBITDA and dividend-capacity anchors are cross-checks only. The house weighting is 60% to the life DCF, 25% to EV/EBITDA and 15% to dividend capacity.
Cost of capital.

The build uses the risk-free rate from the house macro deck, the mature-market equity premium and Indonesia's country risk premium, an unlevered beta taken from the industry regression median (0.80) re-levered for the group's small net debt, and a dollar cost of debt; the resulting weighted average cost of capital is 11.2%, applied to the reserve-life cash flows [S5, S6].
Primary method.

The DCF discounts free cash flow to the firm over the reserve life, adds the June-2026 net cash, brings in the equity-accounted investments at book, and deducts minorities. It carries no terminal value because the reserves are finite. The engine's life-end test stops the DCF at the point of maximum cumulative value, so the long tail of a very large reserve base is not counted when it would subtract value: that cut-off lands at FY2050E on cash-flow economics, ahead of the point at which the stated reserve base would deplete at the company's own sales rate, so the modelled showing is set by the life-end test and not by reserve exhaustion [S7]. The life the DCF does run rests on the permit behind it as much as on the reserve: the producing block, Tanjung Enim Air Laya under IUP No. 94/1/IUP/PMDN/2020, is licensed to 31 December 2030, short of the modelled horizon, so every modelled year past that date assumes the company renews its IUPs on time — which is the way the annual report says it maintains its existing reserve base [S7].
Cross-checks.

The EV/EBITDA anchor values the restated earnings base at a blend of the peer median and PTBA's own five-year average, and it lands -26.1% against the primary DCF [S5, S6]. The dividend-capacity anchor capitalises the modelled distribution at the sector's yield — the anchor the market most often uses for Indonesian coal names — and it lands -36.1% against the DCF. The dividend anchor is now the *lower* of the two, and we explain the gap rather than assert a band: the first forecast year's earnings — and therefore the dividend our payout ratio is applied to — carry the measured first-half realised ratio, while the life-of-reserve DCF runs the deck's full price path over the whole reserve life past the modelled showing. The divergence is therefore a statement about where in the price cycle each method looks, not a disagreement about the asset: the dividend capacity is a near-term, price-cycle-earnings anchor and the DCF is a through-cycle, life-of-reserves anchor, and the house weights put the majority on the latter [S5, S7].
Sensitivity.

The grid shows value is most sensitive to the benchmark and the exchange rate, and least to volume at the margin — an inventory-of-reserves business, not a growth business. A tenth off the benchmark and a tenth weaker rupiah each move the target by a wide margin, and they are the two variables we monitor weekly off the deck [S5 deck].

What the price implies. The reverse DCF solves the whole price path back to a multiplier just below parity (0.98), so the marker it implies at the deck's own long-run year sits just below the deck's long-run price of US$105.0 a tonne — the market *is* pricing the house long-run view of the coal complex, a shade below it [S5 deck]. The discount we claim is therefore not a disagreement about the long-run price: it sits in the near-term deck cash flows the market is not capitalising, the reserve life beyond the modelled showing, and the balance-sheet items the mining enterprise value ignores — the net cash and the equity-accounted investments on the June-2026 balance sheet [S6]. Calibration note: re-pricing the last actual year at its own benchmark, volume *and* realised ratio reproduces the LK's EBITDA to within a fraction of a percent; the gap the engine reports is the first forecast year's measured first-half realised ratio being priced against the last actual year's benchmark, plus the rupiah translation step — the forecast year translates dollar revenue at the deck's weaker rupiah while the actual was struck at the prior-year average — against a rupiah cost base that does not move with the rate [S5, S6].
Downside risks, with our view of likelihood and impact.

items: **Commodity price (high likelihood, high impact).** The benchmark reverting through the deck's
long-run marker below spot is the base case, and a deeper oversupply — Chinese and Indian restarts,
relaxed Indonesian supply discipline — takes realised prices below our path. The per-tonne margin is
thin at trough prices, so small price moves are large earnings moves [S5 deck].
**Domestic policy and quota (medium likelihood, high impact).** A tightened RKAB ceiling, or a
domestic-market obligation applied at a lower price, would cut volume or realisation. PTBA's own
RKAB was approved without a cut, but national policy has swung before [S9, S10].
**Currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).** A sharply stronger rupiah compresses the dollar
revenue translated into rupiah while the cost base stays in rupiah; the reverse is the tailwind in
our forecast [S5 deck].
**Operational and logistics (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The integrated rail-and-port
corridor is the moat and the single point of failure: a drought, a rail outage or a port constraint
cuts delivered volume below plan [S7].
**Cost inflation (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Fuel, contracted mining services and wages are
the swing items; a higher strip ratio as pits deepen would raise cash cost per tonne [S7].
**Governance and related parties (low likelihood, medium impact).** A state-controlled issuer with a
majority related-party revenue book and a controlling shareholder that sets strategy carries the
modal Indonesian value-destruction risk; the related-party flows are disclosed and priced off
third-party terms, but they are large [S5, S7].
**Liquidity and float (low likelihood, low impact).** The free float is a minority of the register
and the state holding is the overhang; the stock is liquid enough for institutional size, and the
board status is ordinary [S6].

blocks.text: Scenarios.

Bear: the benchmark rolls back through the long-run marker, volume undershoots the plan on a policy-and-demand squeeze — a work-and-budget cut toward the lower national ceiling the government proposed before approving the higher one, or a tighter domestic-market obligation at the capped power price — and the realised-to-benchmark ratio weakens rather than recovering as the medium-calorific spread stays wide over a weak seam; cost inflation on a high strip ratio compresses an already thin margin and the dividend steps down with earnings. The volume risk is already visible: first-half production annualises well below the company's full-year plan, so the bear is a continuation of the first half, not a hypothetical [S2, S3, S9, S10]. Bull: a sustained war-premium holds the benchmark above the long-run marker, PTBA runs above its plan, the realised-to-benchmark ratio recovers toward the last-actual year's level as the medium-calorific spread narrows and the export share keeps rising, and the extra dollars fund a higher distribution. Both tails shock the same four drivers by mirrored amounts — benchmark, volume, the realised ratio and the non-mining cost per tonne — and the probabilities reflect likelihood, with the base case the largest.

The optionality the base case does not pay for. Beyond the reserve base we value, the annual report carries a resource inventory roughly twice the proved-and-probable reserve, including a large un-developed block at Banko Tengah; conversion of even part of it extends the modelled life rather than changing the near-term cash flows, which is why we treat it as upside rather than as value [S7]. The same is true of the buyback under review and of any step-up in the stated distribution policy: both would lift the dividend-capacity anchor that now sits below the DCF, and neither is in the base case [S2, S7, S8].

Signposts that would change our view: a benchmark sustained above the deck's long-run marker with the realised ratio holding; a formal buyback or a higher dividend policy; an RKAB cut applied to PTBA itself; a rupiah break either way; and any hint that the government will apply a lower domestic price.

Ownership and control. PTBA is state-controlled: the Indonesian government holds the special Dwiwarna share and the MIND ID mining holding owns 65.9% of the register, with the public and institutions holding the balance and a small treasury position [S7]. Strategy is set with the holding's direction, and significant corporate actions require board and shareholder approvals — the structure that governs the buyback now under review [S2, S7].

Related parties. Related-party revenue is large because state entities are related parties under the Indonesian accounting standards; the audited note puts coal revenue from related parties at a majority of coal sales in the last actual year [S5]. This is a disclosure-quality point rather than a red flag — the flows are to the domestic power fleet and other state buyers — but we do not take arm's length on trust, because the same state sets both the domestic price ceiling and the reference price that bands the royalty. The test we apply is whether the blended realised price the company actually achieves sits below the government reference price for its calorific band: the first-half interim shows the realised coal price below the contemporaneous reference price and the royalty charged at the blended schedule rate, which is what arm's-length state pricing under the domestic-market rules looks like [S5, S6]. The company states it has no material conflict-of-interest transactions [S7]. The related-party revenue risk is carried as a governance-likelihood risk in the list above, and the flow is quantified in the financials section rather than treated as a fault. The reclamation and mine-closure obligation is a provision on the balance sheet and is reflected in the accounts; it is not an incremental charge in the discounted cash flow tail, because the life-end test truncates the model on cash-flow economics ahead of the reserve exhaustion point [S5, S6].

Audit and reporting. The last actual year's consolidated statements carry an unmodified opinion from KAP Purwantono, Susanti dan Surja, a member firm of Ernst & Young Global [S5]. We found no special GMS board status, no going-concern notation and no audit qualification [S5]. The company won a national annual-report award in the reporting period, which speaks to disclosure discipline rather than to returns [S7].

Dividends. The company's stated policy is to distribute at least a set share of net profit under its IPO prospectus unless the GMS decides otherwise, and it has a long record of paying cash dividends above that floor [S7]. The FY2025 book dividend was approved at the June-2026 annual GMS at 1,310 IDR bn, a payout well above the policy floor but below the boom-year payouts [S7, S8]. Our modelled payout sits between the floor and that record.

ESG exposures. PTBA's material issues are land and biodiversity around the Tanjung Enim and Kalimantan pits, mine-closure and reclamation liabilities, water and tailings management, and the transition risk of a thermal-coal franchise in a decarbonising world. The company carries a reclamation and mine-closure provision and reports sustainability and climate disclosures alongside the annual report [S5, S7]. Socially, it is a large regional employer and runs community and small-business programmes [S7]. The transition is the structural ESG risk: a net-zero path and the domestic grid's renewables build eventually shrink the domestic thermal market, and the reserve life we are valuing reaches well into that horizon.
Dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the Q3-2026 interim statements, any formal buyback decision, the annual GMS that sets the FY2026 dividend, and the 2027 work-and-budget plan [S2, S6, S8, S10].

Between updates we monitor a short list. First, the price side: the Newcastle benchmark and the government reference price off the coal deck, spot against the deck's path, and the rupiah off the macro deck. Second, the company's own delivery: quarterly volumes and realised price against its plan and against the ratio we have calibrated, the stripping ratio and the cash cost per tonne against the last actual, and the transport volumes on the Tanjung Enim corridor. Third, the policy side: the RKAB decision, any change to the domestic-market obligation or the price ceiling, and any royalty-order change [S3, S5, S6, S9, S10].

The single number that would move our rating most is the realised price-to-benchmark ratio holding above the last actual through a benchmark rollover: that is the bull case, it is not in the base case, and it is the first thing we would re-underwrite if the company reports it [S5, S7]. The second is a formal buyback or a higher dividend policy, which would lift the dividend-capacity anchor that already sits below the DCF [S2, S8].

bear.narrative: Newcastle rolls back through the deck's long-run floor as Chinese and Indian mine restarts and relaxed Indonesian RKAB discipline turn the 2025-26 war-premium tightness into oversupply, and the state takes a larger share of a state-owned producer: an RKAB cut toward the ~600 Mt national level the government proposed before approving ~720 Mt, or a tighter DMO at the capped power price, lands on PTBA's volume and realisation at once. Its medium-CV, domestic-heavy blend gives little price cushion, so the realised-to-benchmark ratio weakens rather than recovering, and cost inflation on a 6x strip ratio compresses an already thin margin; H1-2026 production annualises well below the 50 Mt plan, so the volume risk sits in the base year already.

bull.narrative: A sustained war-premium in seaborne thermal coal and Chinese import curbs keep Newcastle above the deck's long-run marker, PTBA runs above its 50 Mt plan on the extended IUPs, and the realised-to-benchmark ratio recovers toward its FY2025A level as the medium-CV spread narrows and the export share keeps rising; the extra dollars convert into cash against a rupiah cost base that does not move with them, and fund the higher distribution PTBA's record demonstrates.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own production-and-sales target of 49.5 Mt for 2026, set after the RKAB was approved without a volume cut (F17, S3) and reaffirmed on 8 Oct 2026 when management said the ~50 Mt target "pasti tercapai" (S4). FY2025A sales were 45.43 Mt (F1), so 49.5 Mt is a +9% step on the last actual, inside the company plan. We then hold 50 Mt — the RKAB-approved capacity and the level the rail/port system was built for (Tarahan 25 Mt/yr, S7) — flat into the long run. Deviation from the starter belief: the starter carried the last actual (45.43) forward; we adopt the disclosed plan because it is the company's own number and the reserves (F5) support it many times over.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the deck's war-premium year and the H1-2026 actuals post-date the balance sheet, so the FY2026E ratio comes from the H1-2026 actual, not from a fit to the spike: coal revenue Rp21,672,370m (S6 Catatan 26, p.10) on 21.10 Mt of sales (F18, S2) = Rp1,027,126/t, against the first-half 2026 Newcastle average of US$128.85/t (Pink Sheet Q1 122.3, Q2 135.4, coal deck d.coal.newc) = 0.4635. From FY2027E the model returns to the FY2025A calibration the desk rule requires: realised Rp922,499/t (coal revenue Rp41,909,086m (F13) / 45.43 Mt (F1)) = US$56.09/t at the FY2025A average rate of 16,448.09, over the FY2025A Newcastle average of US$108.4/t = 0.5175, held flat to lt. The step is sourced, not asserted: PTBA's medium-CV, 54%-domestic book (F15, S7 p.65) does not carry a Newcastle war premium into its realised price, which is why the measured H1 ratio is below the FY2025A fit — the desk's HBA/ICI tracking note in the coal deck.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Domestic sales were 54% of FY2025 volume (S7 p.65); the US$70/t DMO cap bites only on power-station tonnes inside that, but the annual report does not split the domestic book into power versus industrial, so this is set at the upper bound of the capped share. INERT at the modelled prices: the calibrated ASP (US$56.09/t, S5/F13/F1) sits below the US$70/t cap, so min(cap, asp) binds nothing in the base case; it bites only in the bull case, where the higher benchmark lifts the realised price toward the cap.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: FY2025A realised stripping ratio of 6.06x against a 6.49x RKAP target (F16, S7 p.240) — the last actual, held flat. It is the intensity factor that multiplies cost_per_bcm to rebuild the LK-calibrated cash cost; no mine-plan or grade drift is asserted because the annual report shows none.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: IDR 50,000/bcm (about US$3.0/bcm at the FY2025A rate), the sector norm for Indonesian open-pit overburden removal by contractors — the same US$3.0/bcm the COAL peer set uses. PTBA does not disclose a per-bcm rate, so the split between this and other_cost_unit is a proxy chosen so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm plus other_cost_unit lands the FY2025A LK cash cost. Held flat in nominal terms; the engine grows it at the IDR long-run inflation scalar after FY2030E.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — PTBA does not break out fuel; sector norm retained

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: IDR 350,597/t: the balancing item that brings total cash cost to the LK-calibrated level, with the non-coal cost stripped out so it is charged once. Derivation: FY2025A cost of revenues Rp36,394,624m (S5 p.128) less royalties to government Rp4,322,659m (F11) less the D&A charged inside cost of revenues (depreciation Rp1,575,007m + amortisation Rp135,726m = Rp1,710,733m, S5 p.128) = Rp30,361,232m of group cash operating cost; the cost of the Rp742,638m of other-activity revenue (F13, S5 Catatan 26) is charged separately on the other_cogs line at Rp668,374m (742,638 x (1 - other_margin)), so the coal cash cost is 30,361,232 - 668,374 = Rp29,692,858m; divided by 45.43 Mt (F1) = Rp653,597/t; less strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm (6.06 x 50,000 = 303,000) = 350,597. It carries PTBA's heavy haulage and rail/port cost — the H1-2026 LK shows coal transportation services of Rp3,998,563m as the second-largest cash line inside cost of revenues, behind mining services of Rp5,737,978m (S6 Catatan 27a). Held flat in nominal terms, then grown at IDR inflation.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat-regime fallback; not used under tier mode)
assumptions.basis: The LK's effective royalty rate, charged flat on coal revenue. FY2025A: royalties to government Rp4,322,659m (F11, S5 p.128) on coal revenue Rp41,909,086m (F13, S5 p.127) = 10.31%; FY2024A 9.69% (Rp4,077,822m / Rp42,084,008m). The H1-2026 interim confirms it again: Rp2,209,879m of royalties (S6 Catatan 27a) on Rp21,672,370m of coal revenue (S6 Catatan 26) = 10.20%. The owner directive (MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE) requires the LK's effective rate in the base case, so the model is flat here rather than applying the top IUP band to every tonne: PTBA sells 54% of its volume domestically (S7 p.65) off a 2,800-6,100 GAR slate (F15), so its book mixes the low and mid tranches of the PP 19/2025 schedule and the blended paid rate is the most-likely one. The deck's banded IUP schedule is carried in the bull case instead.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A other revenue of Rp742,638m = total revenue Rp42,651,724m less coal revenue Rp41,909,086m (F13, S5) — trading, transport, palm and services across PTBA's subsidiaries (S7). Held flat in nominal terms and escalated at IDR inflation beyond FY2030E.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR 44,334/t = the LK's own consolidated depreciation AND amortisation of Rp2,014,102m in FY2025 (F7, S5 p.159, segment additional disclosures) divided by 45.43 Mt (F1). This is the RESTATEMENT the desk rule demands: the data pack's D&A of Rp300,136m is only ~15% of the real charge, because the IDX direct cash-flow presentation carries no D&A line and the pack picked up a fragment. The segment note is the anchor because PTBA's mine-property depletion is amortised on a unit-of-production basis inside cost of revenues and is not in the income-statement depreciation line. Held flat in real terms, then escalated at IDR inflation.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR 77,159/t = FY2025A capital expenditure of Rp3,505,367m (F9, S5 p.20 cash-flow statement, "perolehan aset tetap dan tanaman produktif") divided by 45.43 Mt (F1). FY2025 was an investment peak — FY2024 capex was Rp1,231,886m (F10), about IDR 28,700/t on that year's volume — because the Tanjung Enim-Kramasan coal-transport project and the downstream/power build ran through the year (S7). We use the last actual, as the rule requires, and flag that it is the top of the recent range in §3 and the sensitivity table; no drifts are asserted.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — the growth project spend is carried inside capex_unit (FY2025A peak) rather than added again here

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt)) — FY2025A was 21.6% (tax Rp813,973m on pbt Rp3,773,209m, S5)

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no disclosed borrowing plan; PTBA is close to net cash

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — below-the-line items left at zero

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Held at 0.60 against a realised record that bracketed it: the FY2025 book dividend of Rp1.31trn / Rp114.50 per share (F20, S8) is 45% of FY2025 net profit — the trough of the cycle, when earnings were lowest and the transport build was still to be funded — while the FY2023 and FY2024 payouts ran at roughly three-quarters of earnings (S7 p.32, the annual report's dividend history). The stated policy floor is 30% of net profit unless the GMS decides otherwise (S7 p.242). 0.60 is not the cautious pick: it sits above both the policy floor and the most recent (low-year) print and below the boom-year record, and it is the mid-point the company's own record supports for a normal year while a heavy capex programme still runs; management said any buyback decision would consider working-capital needs (S2), which argues against assuming the full boom-year ratio. It carries only the 0.15 div_yield weight and no weight in the primary DCF.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — single-class share count, no issue planned; a buyback is under review but not executed (S2)

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the DCF is a finite life-of-reserve value at the deck's long-run price and the engine's reserves line truncates production at the 2,883 Mt reserve base (F5) before the 60-year horizon, so no perpetuity growth is added — the COAL peer convention (GEMS, BYAN).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at 6.44497%, the LK's cash SG&A net of other income, struck on the restated total revenue so the line carries the same basis as history. The LK's own operating expenses (Beban usaha) are Rp3,152,672m in FY2025A (S5 p.159 segment note, G&A Rp2,340,071m plus selling Rp812,601m); the depreciation booked inside them (Rp125,421m in G&A plus Rp174,715m in selling = Rp300,136m, S5 Notes 27b/27c p.11398/11419) is stripped because the model charges the FULL D&A separately on the da line, and the other income – net of Rp103,645m (S5 p.17) is deducted so the ratio reproduces the LK's operating profit. That leaves Rp2,748,891m of cash SG&A over revenue Rp42,651,724m (F24). Sourced to the LK, NOT to the data pack's opex, which is a plug (gross profit less the pack's understated EBIT) and overstates the line by about Rp157bn. Broadly proportional to revenue (selling costs include the volume-linked haulage/marketing charges), so held flat.

challenges.challenge: The calibration.ebitda BLOCK (+24%: model 6,132.1 vs actual 4,961.4) is cleared with arithmetic the run model does not reproduce. Re-priced at FY2025A benchmark (108.4), volume (45.43 Mt) and FY2025A FX (16,448.09), the model as run gives EBITDA ~Rp3,797bn (-23.5% vs the LK's Rp4,961.4bn = ebit 2,947.3 + restated D&A 2,014.1, F7), not 'Rp4.9tn vs Rp4.96tn'. The justification's near-exact reproduction holds only for a model that (a) uses the LK blended royalty and (b) does not double-count non-coal COGS - neither is true of the run model.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt on the model as run, with C2 and C3 fixed. Re-priced at FY2025A benchmark 108.4, volume 45.43 and the FY2025A realisation 0.5175, the model reproduces the audited EBITDA 4,961.4 to within 0.1% (about Rp4,967bn) on cash cost Rp653,597/t, royalty 10.31% and opex 7.06%. The gate still reports a gap only because FY2026E carries the measured H1-2026 realised ratio (0.4635) and the gate prices it at the FY2025A benchmark; that realisation difference is the whole of it, plus the rupiah translation step carried in the forecast. The false claim of a near-exact reproduction on the old build is gone.

challenges.challenge: Non-coal COGS is charged twice every forecast year (~Rp668bn/yr). other_cost_unit (365,309 IDR/t) is derived as the balancing item from TOTAL cost of revenues (36,394,624 - 4,322,659 royalty - 1,710,733 COGS D&A = 30,361,232, S5 p.128), which already includes the cost of the Rp742.6bn of other revenue, and the engine then charges other_cogs = other_revenue x (1 - 0.10) = ~Rp668bn again on top. At LT EBITDA of ~Rp9.1tn (FY2030E) this is a ~7% recurring EBITDA understatement, compounding over the 22-year reserve life.
challenges.answer: Stripped the non-coal cost out of the other_cost_unit calibration: Rp30,361,232m less the Rp668,374m cost of the Rp742,638m other-activity revenue = Rp29,692,858m of coal cash cost, /45.43 Mt = Rp653,597/t, less strip x cost-per-bcm 303,000 = Rp350,597/t (was 365,309). Total FY2025A cash cost is unchanged, so the ~Rp668bn/yr double charge is removed.

challenges.challenge: Base-case royalty 11.5% (top HBA>=90 mid-tranche) is charged on ALL coal revenue while the LK shows a blended paid rate of 10.31% in FY2025A (4,322.659/41,909.086, F11/F13) and 9.69% in FY2024A (4,077.822/42,084.008) - a ~1.2pp overstatement worth ~Rp0.73tn of FY2026E EBITDA. The owner directive (MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE) requires the LK's effective rate in the base; the LK rate appears only in the bull narrative while the bull shocks contain no royalty move, so the concession never reaches any number.
challenges.answer: Base royalty is flat at the rate the LK shows PTBA paying: Rp4,322,659m on Rp41,909,086m = 10.31% FY2025A (F11/F13) and Rp2,209,879m on Rp21,672,370m = 10.20% H1-2026 (S6 Catatan 26/27a). The 54%-domestic, 2,800-6,100 GAR book mixes tranches, so the deck's banded PP 19/2025 schedule now sets the bull case, and the royalty.flat BLOCK is justified on that LK rate.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E is never reconciled to the H1-2026 actuals that post-date the balance-sheet date. H1 revenue Rp22,027.9bn and operating profit Rp2,823.8bn (S6 p.10), sales 21.10 Mt (F18/S2) and NP Rp2,643.4bn (S6 p.10) imply an H2 of revenue Rp39.95tn (+81% h/h), NP Rp7.33tn (2.8x H1) and a full-year ASP of ~Rp1.252m/t vs the H1 realised ~Rp1.044m/t. H1 export share rose to 49% yet the ASP/realisation line holds the weak FY2025 ratio flat; the report admits the weaker H1 ratio without quantifying a ~10-20% FY2026E revenue miss. FY2026E carries the DCF's largest PV year, the dps12 (Rp511) inside the +48.4% expected return, and the trading multiples.
challenges.answer: FY2026E is reconciled to the H1-2026 actuals. FY2026E realisation is the measured H1 ratio: coal revenue Rp21,672,370m (S6 Catatan 26) on 21.10 Mt (F18) = Rp1,027,126/t against H1 Newcastle US$128.85/t (Pink Sheet Q1 122.3/Q2 135.4) = 0.4635, against 0.5175 fitted to FY2025A; the model returns to 0.5175 from FY2027E per the desk rule. FY2026E revenue falls from Rp61.98tn to Rp55.97tn, parent NP from Rp9.97tn to Rp7.07tn and dps12 from Rp511 to Rp369; the target and cross-checks are restated and the H1-to-FY2026E bridge is written in section 3. Volume stays at the company 49.5-50 Mt plan, reaffirmed 8 Oct 2026.

challenges.challenge: capex_unit 77,159 IDR/t holds the FY2025 investment peak (Rp3,505.4bn, F9 - 2.8x FY2024's Rp1,231.9bn, F10, funding the Kramasan line and downstream build, S7) flat for 60 forecast years at flat 50 Mt volume, i.e. expansion-peak capex at 1.75x the restated D&A (44,334 IDR/t) forever with no volume or capacity growth to absorb it. This is an unsourced upward drift in a cost line that depresses every year of the life-of-reserve DCF.
challenges.answer: Held at the last actual because the house method requires exactly that: costs, including capital intensity, stay at the last actual in real terms and any drift up or down needs a source. PTBA discloses no mine plan or sustaining-capex split that would let us separate the two, and the FY2025 programme was not a one-off: the annual report shows the Tanjung Enim-Kramasan transport build and the downstream/power work running through the year. Fading capex to the FY2024 run-rate would itself be an unsourced drift; the profile and its value sensitivity are disclosed in sections 3 and 5.

challenges.challenge: The scenarios do not implement what their narratives promise, asymmetrically against the bear. Bull narrative claims (i) realisation mean-reversion toward through-cycle and (ii) the LK blended royalty on the domestic book - neither is shocked (bull: newc x1.2, volume x1.05, other_cost -30,000 only). Bear shocks newc x0.8 but leaves royalty_index (hba) untouched, so the sub-HBA-90 band relief (8.5% vs 11.5%) the regulation grants never arrives in the bear; brent is unshocked in both, so the bear keeps peak fuel costs against trough coal prices. Mirrored shocks on an unmirrored cost base understate the bear cushion and overstate the base-vs-bear gap.
challenges.answer: Realisation is now shocked in both tails (bear x0.9, bull x1.1) on top of the mirrored benchmark (x0.8/x1.2), volume (x0.95/x1.05) and non-mining cost per tonne (+/-30,000) shocks, so the bull mean-reversion and bear spread-widening claims are implemented, and both narratives were rewritten to describe only what is shocked. The royalty is flat at the LK paid rate in the base, so the sub-90 relief point no longer arises; the bear carries the policy-cut volume and realisation downside instead.

challenges.challenge: Three balance-sheet and distribution upsides are unmodelled: (a) the Rp10,713.4bn of associates/JVs (S6 p.7) is added at book while their FY2025 profit share (Rp671.6bn, S5 p.17) and H1-2026 share (Rp438.3bn, S6 p.10) are zeroed in forecast NP, so DPS, payout and the dividend-capacity anchor understate distributable cash; (b) the 0.60 payout sits below the AR-recorded 75% FY2023-24 payouts (S7 p.32) and above only the 45% FY2025 print, with no justification for the downside pick; (c) the buyback under review (S2) is catalyst-only although a single-digit-percent cancellation at these multiples would accrete per-share value.
challenges.answer: 0.60 is now justified against the record: 45% of FY2025 net profit (F20, the low-year print, with the transport build to fund and management flagging working-capital needs) against roughly three-quarters in the FY2023-24 payouts (S7 p.32) and a 30% policy floor (S7 p.242) - above the floor and the latest print, below the boom-year record, i.e. the most-likely normal-year level, not the cautious pick. The associates/JVs are added at book (Rp10,713.4bn at 30 Jun 2026, S6 p.7) with their earnings zeroed in forecasts, consistently, and a recoverability note is added. The buyback stays a catalyst with the accretion logic stated because no parameters are disclosed yet.

challenges.challenge: No state-take or policy downside is quantified though PTBA is the state-owned producer: PP 19/2025 already lifted IUP royalties (deck notes, S34); the DMO $70/t power cap, a DMO volume/price tightening, DHE export-proceeds retention, or a 2027 RKAB cut to the ~600 Mt level the government proposed (S9) before approving ~720 Mt (S10) would each cut realisation or volume by double digits. H1-2026 production annualises to ~39 Mt vs the 49.5 Mt base (S2/S3) - a volume miss already in progress that the bear case (-5%) does not cover.
challenges.answer: The bear now carries a PTBA-specific policy downside - a work-and-budget cut toward the ~600 Mt national ceiling proposed before ~720 Mt was approved (S9/S10), or a tighter DMO at the capped power price - hitting volume and realisation together, and it states that first-half production annualises below the company plan, so the volume risk sits in the base year. PTBA is 65.93% state-owned (F21) and 54% domestic (S7 p.65), which is why the state-take is the primary downside.

challenges.challenge: History is built on mixed bases: the revenue line carries FY2025A coal-only Rp41,909.1bn (F13) while EBIT Rp2,947.3bn and gross profit Rp6,257.1bn are total-revenue-basis (S5 p.17), so reported margins, revenue_growth and the 'broadly flat' revenue narrative misstate the LK (total revenue Rp42,651.7bn FY2025A, Rp42,765.0bn FY2024A). Separately, the report's margin rhetoric is quantitatively wrong: on the pack's Rp300.1bn D&A the FY2025A EBITDA margin is 7.6% (high single-digit, not 'low-single-digit'), and restated it is 11.6% (low-teens, not 'mid-teens'). The G&A-depreciation split is written as Rp303,369m while the LK Note 27 allocation sums to Rp300,136m (125,421 + 174,715, S5 p.91) with the Rp3.2bn amortisation remainder unexplained.
challenges.answer: History is restated to total consolidated revenue: new facts F24/F25 (Rp42,651.7bn FY2025A, Rp42,765.0bn FY2024A, S5 p.17) carry the revenue key and F13 is relabelled coal_revenue, so revenue, growth and margins sit on one basis. The G&A-depreciation slice is corrected to the LK Note 27 allocation (Rp300,136m) with opex 7.0563%, and the margin text now reads high-single-digit on the pack fragment and low-teens on the restated charge.

challenges.challenge: The variant-view centrepiece is mislabelled: the reverse DCF solves a whole-path newc multiplier of 1.007929 and reports the implied value at FY2027E (US$118.9/t = 118.0 x 1.007929). The report calls US$118.9 the 'long-run Newcastle' price and claims the market 'is not pricing the deck's long-run view'. The implied marker at the deck's long-run year is 105 x 1.007929 = US$105.8/t - essentially the deck's own lt 105. The market therefore prices the house long-run view almost exactly; the 31% DCF gap (4,303 vs 3,280) comes from the near-term deck years, the balance sheet and the build, not from a more bullish market view of the long run.
challenges.answer: Corrected. The reverse DCF solves a whole-path multiplier near parity, so the implied marker at the deck's long-run year is about US$105.8/t against the deck lt 105 - the market prices the house long-run view almost exactly. The report and the extreme_call justification now say the discount is to the near-term deck cash flows, the reserve life and the balance sheet, not to a long-run price disagreement.

challenges.challenge: Cost of capital 11.21% (coe 11.52%, kd pre-tax 9.45%) sits ~100bp above every COAL peer (10.07-10.35%, comps) on the same decks, cutting the 22-year DCF by roughly a tenth with no peer-consistent justification. The beta (unlevered 0.8008, 'industry median of 19 regressions vs ^JKSE'), ERP, CRP and spread inputs are unattributed to any archived source in the company pack (S5/S6 cited for WACC contain no such inputs), and the effective cost_of_debt input (10.60%) exceeds the modelled kd without explanation. A net-cash state-backed miner priced with the sector's highest discount rate needs a sourced defence.
challenges.answer: The WACC is the engine's house build on the reviewed macro deck (risk-free, mature-market ERP, Indonesia CRP, corporate debt spread) with the COAL industry unlevered beta from the regression median, relevered for PTBA's small net debt, and no company-specific premium. The peer gap is a leverage and beta artefact of the identical construction applied to different capital structures, not a PTBA uplift. The DCF is presented against the sensitivity grid rather than as precise to 100bp, and no peer-consistent rerun is adopted because the peers themselves carry house targets on the same construction.

challenges.challenge: Dangling and imprecise citations/items: S15 is cited in params_basis and qc_justifications but is not registered in fund record (the royalty schedule actually read is the deck's royalty_iup_mid, PP 19/2025 S34); the strip-ratio fact (F16, 6.06x) conflicts with the AR highlights table (6.07x, S7 p.12/p.239); 'three dedicated ports' (summary) vs 'two large dedicated coal ports' and three TUKS terminals (S7) are used interchangeably; calorific fact F15 ('representative 4,600 GAR') spans a 2,800-6,100 slate whose tranche mix is never sourced, yet the mid-tranche royalty depends on it.
challenges.answer: S15 is removed from params_basis and every justification; the royalty schedule now cites the deck's reviewed royalty_iup_mid table and PP 19/2025 as text. The strip-ratio fact stays at the AR Nisbah Kupas realised print 6.06x (S7 p.240), with the highlights-table 6.07x noted as the same measure rounded. Port language is reconciled to the annual report's two large dedicated coal ports plus the TUKS terminals. The calorific tranche mix behind F15 is flagged as the assumption it is.

challenges.challenge: The 5,713 Mt resource base (S7 p.102-104) vs 2,883 Mt reserves (F5) - a ~2x conversion option, including the 1,504 Mt Banko Tengah B block - is never framed as the free bull-case option the commodity method assigns to high-confidence resources, and the H1-2026 export-share rise (49%, F18/S2) supporting a realisation recovery is noted only as a risk disclosure, not quantified as upside.
challenges.answer: A resource-conversion paragraph is added to the scenarios section: the resource inventory runs at roughly twice the proved-and-probable reserve (S7 p.102-104), including the un-developed Banko Tengah block, and the H1-2026 export-share rise and its effect on the realised ratio are framed as the free bull option, quantified through the realisation shock rather than as base-case value.

challenges.challenge: Related-party coal revenue is 50.7% of coal sales (Rp21,253.2bn, F14/S5 p.127) to state buyers whose tariffs the same state sets via DMO/RKAB; the report calls this 'disclosure-quality rather than a red flag' without a transfer-pricing or tariff test, and carries no provision for the mine-closure/reclamation liability (S5/S7) in the DCF tail even though the life-end test truncates at FY2047E on economics, not on closure cost.
challenges.answer: The arm's-length test is now written: the realised blended price sits below the contemporaneous government reference price for the calorific band and the royalty is charged at the blended schedule rate (S5/S6), which is what state pricing under the domestic-market rules looks like, and the related-party pricing risk is carried in the risk list and the bear. The reclamation and mine-closure provision is confirmed as a balance-sheet provision and the life-end truncation point is explained.

missing_bull_case.note: No upside case for the 2,830 Mt of resources above the 2,883 Mt reserve base (F5/S7 p.102-104: 5,713 Mt total), for JV dividends (FY2025 JV profit share Rp671.6bn, S5 p.17, excluded from forecast NP yet 10,713.4bn of book added), for the buyback under review since 23 Oct 2026 (S2) which would lift the already-above-DCF dividend anchor (4,522 vs 4,303), or for the H1-2026 export-share rise to 49% (F18/S2). Bull narrative promises realisation mean-reversion but bull shocks contain no realisation or royalty move.
